title.heading: Great Fire of London
title.lead: Which things in our homes can burn?

picture.shows: A historical illustration of the Great Fire of London
picture.subject: named

slides.heading: The fire begins
slides.lead: The Great Fire of London began in a bakery in Pudding Lane in 1666. A bakery makes bread.

figure.shows: A historical reconstruction of the bakery in Pudding Lane as the fire begins
figure.subject: named

items.question: In which city did the fire begin?
What was the street where the Great Fire began?
In which year did the Great Fire begin?

slides.heading: Why did fire spread?
slides.lead: Wooden houses burned easily. Strong winds blew flames and sparks towards nearby houses, helping the fire spread through London.

figure.shows: A historical illustration showing strong wind blowing flames and sparks from one wooden London house towards another
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Sparks travel in the wind
slides.lead: Sparks are tiny burning pieces. Strong winds carried them to other wooden roofs, where new fires could start.

figure.shows: A close view of wind carrying glowing sparks from a burning wooden roof to an unburnt wooden roof
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Why did strong winds make wooden houses more dangerous?

options.why: The pupil applies the familiar experience of blowing out a candle to a large fire in strong wind.
The pupil thinks moving air cools the houses enough to prevent burning rather than helping flames spread.

slides.heading: Water buckets
slides.lead: People filled leather buckets with water. They carried the water to the fire and threw it onto flames.

figure.shows: People fighting the Great Fire with leather water buckets
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: Pulling down houses
slides.lead: People pulled down some houses before they burned. This made gaps, leaving the fire less wood to burn next.

figure.shows: People using long hooks and ropes to pull down an unburnt wooden house near the Great Fire
figure.subject: named

slides.heading: A gap in the street
slides.lead: A cleared gap left no house to burn next.

figure.shows: A historical reconstruction of burning London houses on one side of a wide cleared gap and standing unburnt houses beyond it
figure.subject: generic

picture.shows: Two imagined streets of wooden houses, one in strong wind and one in still air
picture.subject: generic

items.question: Imagine wooden houses in strong wind. Explain why fire could reach another house.
items.answer: Strong wind could carry flames and sparks to another wooden house.

items.question: Imagine wooden houses without strong wind. Explain why a nearby fire could still spread.
items.answer: The wooden houses could still burn because wood burns easily.

picture.shows: An imagined burning wooden shed near an unburnt wooden house, with leather water buckets nearby
picture.subject: generic

items.question: Imagine a burning shed. Describe how people could fight its flames using buckets.
items.answer: People could fill buckets with water and throw the water onto the flames.

items.question: An empty wooden house stands beside a fire. Explain how destroying it could help.
items.answer: Pulling it down could make a gap so the fire had less wood to burn next.

items.question: Where and when did the Great Fire begin?
How did houses, wind and firefighters affect the fire?
items.answer: Wood burned, wind spread sparks, buckets carried water, and pulling down houses left gaps.
